issues.item: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: For childhood physical abuse by a caregiver, the profile is otherwise organized around shame/self-concept and social avoidance. 'Body Unreliable' is less coherent with the rest of the selected items because there are no accompanying threat or memory items indicating prominent somatic threat, dissociation, injury-related beliefs, or body-based trauma processing. Within this formulation, Negative Appraisals is strongly linked to maladaptive avoidance and modestly linked with triggers; the other appraisals fit that pattern, but this item introduces a distinct body-failure theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Ravi had grown up in a South Asian household where his father's temper was unpredictable and punishment was physical, so that the sound of a door slamming in the next room, or the sting of cold air on his skin, could still feel instantly dangerous to him. At 36, married and working as a detective, he could function for long stretches, but the old fear would arrive with a bodily force that surprised him. He described being caught off guard one winter evening while stepping out of his car at the station: the metal door had swung shut hard behind him, the noise echoing in the garage, and the sharp cold on his wrists had brought him back to the helplessness of childhood. In the hours afterward he found himself thinking, with a familiar wave of shame, that his reactions since all of this showed he was a lousy coper, and that there must be something wrong with him as a person. Each time one of those reminders hit - the slam of a door, the bite of cold on his skin - it did not just frighten Ravi; it immediately hardened into the thought that he was weak and failing to cope, as if the reminder itself proved he was fundamentally defective. What unsettled him most was not only the intensity of the reaction, but the way it made him feel split from himself, as though he did not know himself anymore. The reminders themselves seemed to bring the judgment with them, so that the sound or the sensation arrived already carrying the conclusion that he was a lousy coper and somehow damaged beyond what other people would have to endure. Once that thought took hold, even neutral moments - a car door in the garage, a gust of cold in the parking lot, someone moving behind him - began to feel like fresh evidence that the world was still testing him. Once the door slam or the sharp cold had caught him, Ravi found the judgment arriving with it: that a man who reacted like this must be a lousy coper, someone fundamentally brittle rather than merely startled.

Over time, these moments became the lens through which he judged his entire life. A night when his wife was away and he had to sleep alone in the master bedroom left him staring at the ceiling until nearly dawn, convinced that if he drifted off in an unfamiliar or empty house he would lose his guard and something would happen. The more these episodes seemed to expose him, the more he believed that there was something fundamentally defective in him, and that he was failing at being the sort of man, husband, and detective he had always assumed he should be. That conviction changed what he noticed; once he had come to believe he could not trust himself, ordinary things in the station garage, on the street, or in the house began to snag his attention as possible warnings instead of fading into the background. Because he expected danger and failure in himself, those same ordinary moments felt loaded before they were even fully there, as if his own doubt primed him to catch on every door slam, every draft of cold air, and every movement in his periphery. What had once been background noise now arrived as a signal, and Ravi found that his fear kept selecting the very cues that matched his worst beliefs. That appraisal did not stay abstract: it pushed him to avoid other people whenever he could, to turn down invitations, to keep conversations at work brief, and to find excuses not to go out after hours. The avoidance itself began to create new reminders; each cancelled plan, each empty evening at home, and each altered route around the station garage drew a sharper outline around what he was trying not to think about, so that the life he was shrinking became another daily prompt to the same fear and shame. The way he managed his days also produced its own reminders: the long way he took around the garage, the habit of staying inside after dark, and the empty stretches at home all kept placing him back in contact with what he was avoiding. In that sense, the avoidance did not erase the cues; it scattered them through his routine, until even his efforts to stay safe were constantly pointing him back toward the memory of being caught off guard. He would say he was tired or busy, but privately he felt safer with distance, because being around others made him fear that they might notice how shaken and unlike himself he had become. Yet the very fact that he kept shrinking his life in this way fed the same harsh conclusion, because each cancelled plan and each carefully managed conversation felt like fresh evidence that he could not cope without backing away. As Ravi came to see himself as a lousy coper, ordinary moments also started to snag his attention in ways they had not before, so that a door closing somewhere down the hall, a gust of cold air outside the station, or even the sound of someone moving behind him could suddenly feel like another warning that he was not holding himself together.

Yet the same habits that gave him momentary relief also fed the very fears he was trying to outrun. By staying up until very late, he could postpone the vulnerable moment of sleep, especially if he was alone, but the next day he was more drained and more on edge, and that fatigue made him even quicker to judge himself as a lousy coper. The longer he isolated himself, the less familiar his own responses felt, and the more convinced he became that something was wrong with him at his core. When he finally did go out, even something ordinary like walking from the parking lot into a store could feel loaded: a sudden door banging behind him, or cold wind striking his hands, would jolt him back into that same old certainty that he was not handling things properly and could not trust himself to stay composed. In that state he began reading every reaction as proof of damage, and each fresh surge of shame made the next retreat feel necessary.

At work, Ravi tried to preserve the image of control, but the pattern was narrowing his life. He was avoiding people more than he admitted, arranging his schedule to reduce time with colleagues, and declining social plans with his wife until she started noticing how often he was absent even when he was home. He hated how much effort it took to keep ordinary life at a distance, yet he also feared that if he stopped avoiding, he would be exposed as weak and broken. By the time he sought help, the strain had built into a quiet crisis: he was exhausted from delaying sleep, increasingly cut off from others, and frightened by how quickly a slammed door or a certain temperature against his skin could bring back the same judgments about himself. His avoidance had also drawn the world into the shape of the event, so that the station garage, his own driveway, and the moments at night when he put off going to bed all carried an extra charge, each one making the old reminders easier to meet and harder to dismiss. What brought him in was the fear that he was losing not only sleep, but his sense of who he was, and what he was most hoping for was a way to feel like himself again without having to keep backing away from everyone and everything around him.

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Ravi had grown up in a South Asian household where his father’s temper was unpredictable and punishment was physical, so that the sound of a door slamming in the next room, or the sting of cold air on his skin, could still feel instantly dangerous to him. At 36, married and working as a detective, he could function for long stretches, but the old fear would arrive with a bodily force that surprised him. He described being caught off guard one winter evening while stepping out of his car at the station: the metal door had swung shut hard behind him, the noise echoing in the garage, and the sharp cold on his wrists had brought him back to the helplessness of childhood. In the hours afterward he found himself thinking, with a familiar wave of shame, that his reactions since all of this showed he was a lousy coper, and that there must be something wrong with him as a person. Each time one of those reminders hit — the slam of a door, the bite of cold on his skin — it did not just frighten Ravi; it immediately hardened into the thought that he was weak and failing to cope, as if the reminder itself proved he was fundamentally defective. What unsettled him most was not only the intensity of the reaction, but the way it made him feel split from himself, as though he did not know himself anymore. The reminders themselves seemed to bring the judgment with them, so that the sound or the sensation arrived already carrying the conclusion that he was a lousy coper and somehow damaged beyond what other people would have to endure. Once that thought took hold, even neutral moments — a car door in the garage, a gust of cold in the parking lot, someone moving behind him — began to feel like fresh evidence that the world was still testing him. Once the door slam or the sharp cold had caught him, Ravi found the judgment arriving with it: that a man who reacted like this must be a lousy coper, someone fundamentally brittle rather than merely startled.

Over time, these moments became the lens through which he judged his entire life. A night when his wife was away and he had to sleep alone in the master bedroom left him staring at the ceiling until nearly dawn, convinced that if he drifted off in an unfamiliar or empty house he would lose his guard and something would happen. The more these episodes seemed to expose him, the more he believed that there was something fundamentally defective in him, and that he was failing at being the sort of man, husband, and detective he had always assumed he should be. That conviction changed what he noticed; once he had come to believe he could not trust himself, ordinary things in the station garage, on the street, or in the house began to snag his attention as possible warnings instead of fading into the background. Because he expected danger and failure in himself, those same ordinary moments felt loaded before they were even fully there, as if his own doubt primed him to catch on every door slam, every draft of cold air, and every movement in his periphery. What had once been background noise now arrived as a signal, and Ravi found that his fear kept selecting the very cues that matched his worst beliefs. That appraisal did not stay abstract: it pushed him to avoid other people whenever he could, to turn down invitations, to keep conversations at work brief, and to find excuses not to go out after hours. The avoidance itself began to create new reminders; each cancelled plan, each empty evening at home, and each altered route around the station garage drew a sharper outline around what he was trying not to think about, so that the life he was shrinking became another daily prompt to the same fear and shame. The way he managed his days also produced its own reminders: the long way he took around the garage, the habit of staying inside after dark, and the empty stretches at home all kept placing him back in contact with what he was avoiding. In that sense, the avoidance did not erase the cues; it scattered them through his routine, until even his efforts to stay safe were constantly pointing him back toward the memory of being caught off guard. He would say he was tired or busy, but privately he felt safer with distance, because being around others made him fear that they might notice how shaken and unlike himself he had become. Yet the very fact that he kept shrinking his life in this way fed the same harsh conclusion, because each cancelled plan and each carefully managed conversation felt like fresh evidence that he could not cope without backing away. As Ravi came to see himself as a lousy coper, ordinary moments also started to snag his attention in ways they had not before, so that a door closing somewhere down the hall, a gust of cold air outside the station, or even the sound of someone moving behind him could suddenly feel like another warning that he was not holding himself together.

Yet the same habits that gave him momentary relief also fed the very fears he was trying to outrun. By staying up until very late, he could postpone the vulnerable moment of sleep, especially if he was alone, but the next day he was more drained and more on edge, and that fatigue made him even quicker to judge himself as a lousy coper. The longer he isolated himself, the less familiar his own responses felt, and the more convinced he became that something was wrong with him at his core. When he finally did go out, even something ordinary like walking from the parking lot into a store could feel loaded: a sudden door banging behind him, or cold wind striking his hands, would jolt him back into that same old certainty that he was not handling things properly and could not trust himself to stay composed. In that state he began reading every reaction as proof of damage, and each fresh surge of shame made the next retreat feel necessary.

At work, Ravi tried to preserve the image of control, but the pattern was narrowing his life. He was avoiding people more than he admitted, arranging his schedule to reduce time with colleagues, and declining social plans with his wife until she started noticing how often he was absent even when he was home. He hated how much effort it took to keep ordinary life at a distance, yet he also feared that if he stopped avoiding, he would be exposed as weak and broken. By the time he sought help, the strain had built into a quiet crisis: he was exhausted from delaying sleep, increasingly cut off from others, and frightened by how quickly a slammed door or a certain temperature against his skin could bring back the same judgments about himself. His avoidance had also drawn the world into the shape of the event, so that the station garage, his own driveway, and the moments at night when he put off going to bed all carried an extra charge, each one making the old reminders easier to meet and harder to dismiss. What brought him in was the fear that he was losing not only sleep, but his sense of who he was, and what he was most hoping for was a way to feel like himself again without having to keep backing away from everyone and everything around him.
